title: Matching and Simplifying Charts for an Audience
summary: Learn to choose the right chart type for the specific point you are making to a stakeholder audience, then simplify that chart by removing visual clutter so the operations manager can focus on the finding, not on reading the graph.

steps.title: The chart must match the point, not just the data
steps.lede: You have the delivery data. The question is: which chart makes your specific point land for the operations manager?

blocks.text: During your own exploration you might have built a bar chart, a line plot, and a boxplot of the delivery data. Presenting to the operations manager, the question changes: which one actually makes the Lagos point, for this audience? The same dataset can support several chart types — the right choice depends on the specific point you are communicating, not on the data alone.

A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories — showing average delivery time side by side across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano. A line graph is best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time — showing Lagos delivery time rising week over week. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing distributions side by side, but a boxplot may be unfamiliar to many people and could introduce a learning curve; for a manager who hasn't seen one before, a bar chart or line plot can often make the point more directly.

steps.title: Why the chart type must match the point you are making
steps.lede: Watch how the same data looks different depending on chart type, and notice when a chart makes comparison easy versus hard.

blocks.group_title: Why the chart type must match the point you are making

segments.label: Bar chart vs. pie chart: comparing values across categories
segments.summary: The same time-use data (sleep, work, eat, rest) is shown first as a pie chart, then as a bar chart. The pie makes it hard to judge which slice is larger when two slices are close in size. The bar chart, with its common baseline, makes the one-hour difference between working and sleeping immediately readable. A second example pits two pie charts against a grouped bar chart to answer 'does Earl work more than Herman, and by how much?' — a question the pies struggle to answer and the bar chart resolves at a glance.

segments.label: Boxplots: strong for distributions, but risky with unfamiliar audiences
segments.summary: A boxplot is considered as a candidate for showing distributions across multiple groups. Two practical problems emerge: sparse data on some days would produce boxes with no box body, and — more broadly — boxplots are not a widely recognised chart type, so an audience unfamiliar with them faces a steeper learning curve. The presenter notes that a specialist audience (researchers and physicians) may be the exception, but still sets the boxplot aside in favour of continuing to explore other options.

bridge.before: Watch how the same data looks different depending on chart type, and notice when a chart makes comparison easy versus hard. The first clip argues strongly for bars over pies; Devspace's text also covers when a pie is the right choice.
bridge.after: The first clip demonstrates f1 and counters the pie-slice comparison misconception; the second covers f3 and f5. Neither clip addresses part-to-whole framing (f4) or scatterplots (f6) — the text covers both.

steps.title: Pie charts, scatterplots, and the comparison trap
steps.lede: Two more chart types complete the toolkit — and one common misconception about pie charts is worth clearing up.

blocks.text: A pie chart expresses a part-to-whole relationship in the data. It is best used either for a general sense of how parts relate to the whole, or to highlight that one segment is notably larger or smaller than the others. The pie must depict a meaningful whole — values that sum to 100%. If the point is 'Lagos accounts for most of our total delivery volume,' a pie chart of each city's share of total orders fits that part-to-whole framing in a way a bar chart of averages would not.

A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, though it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience. Keep this in mind if the distance/delivery-time relationship ever needs to go in front of the manager directly, rather than staying an exploratory chart.

It can look like comparing pie slices is just as easy as comparing bar lengths, since both show a value at a glance — but it is not. A bar chart's aligned, common baseline makes length differences easy to judge; two pie slices of similar size are harder to rank correctly by eye.

steps.title: Scatterplot: exploratory or communicative?
steps.lede: Test your understanding of when a scatterplot is the right choice for a stakeholder audience.

public.prompt: A data analyst plots distance_km against delivery_minutes for all orders across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano. Which statement best describes how a scatterplot is typically used?

options.text: A scatterplot is primarily used to understand data during exploration, though it can be designed to communicate findings to an audience.
A scatterplot is the clearest chart for communicating findings to a non-technical audience because it shows every individual data point.
A scatterplot cannot be used to communicate findings to an audience under any circumstances.
A scatterplot is best used to show how a value changes over time.

opt_a.message: Correct. A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, but it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience.

opt_b.message: Incorrect. Showing every individual data point makes a scatterplot harder, not easier, for a non-technical audience to read without extra design work such as a clear title, colour coding, and a trend line.

opt_c.message: Incorrect. A scatterplot can be designed to communicate findings to an audience — it just requires deliberate choices such as a clear title and colour coding. The default is exploratory, not the only use.

opt_d.message: Incorrect. Showing change over time is the strength of a line graph, not a scatterplot. A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables.

correct.message: Right. Scatterplots are exploratory by default — they reveal relationships in your own analysis. With deliberate design choices they can communicate findings to an audience, but that extra work is required.

incorrect.message: A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, though it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience.

hints: Think about who typically reads a scatterplot — the analyst building it, or the manager receiving the report?
The fact says 'often used to understand data' — does that mean it can never communicate?

steps.title: Match the chart to the stakeholder point
steps.lede: Given a stakeholder point about the delivery data, choose the chart type that best communicates it and explain why.

public.prompt: The operations manager needs three separate charts for three different points. Drag each stakeholder point into the bucket for the chart type that best communicates it.

items.text: "Lagos has the longest average delivery time compared with Abuja and Kano."
"Lagos average delivery time has been rising week over week for the past eight weeks."
"Lagos accounts for most of our total delivery volume across all three cities."
"The spread of individual delivery times differs across cities — some cities have much more variation than others."
"There may be a relationship between distance from the depot and delivery time."

item_comparison.message: A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories — perfect for a side-by-side city comparison.

item_trend.message: Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time, making the week-over-week rise in Lagos immediately visible.

item_part_whole.message: A pie chart expresses a part-to-whole relationship — Lagos's share of total orders sums to 100% with the other cities, making this the right framing.

item_distribution.message: Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing distributions side by side, but may be unfamiliar to many people and could introduce a learning curve — flag this for a non-technical audience.

item_relationship.message: A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. It can convey the distance/delivery-time relationship, but requires deliberate design choices for a non-technical audience.

correct.message: Well done. Each chart type matches the specific point: bar for comparison, line for trend, pie for part-to-whole, boxplot for distribution (with an audience caveat), and scatterplot for relationships (exploratory by default).

incorrect.message: The chart type must match the specific point being made. Bar = comparison across categories; line = change over time; pie = part-to-whole (must sum to 100%); boxplot = distributions (risky with non-technical audiences); scatterplot = relationships (exploratory by default).

hints: Ask yourself: is the point about comparing categories, showing change over time, or showing how parts add up to a whole?
For the distribution item, think about whether the operations manager has seen a boxplot before.

steps.title: Remove the clutter — not the data
steps.lede: A chart built for your own exploration carries elements the operations manager doesn't need. Each removal reduces reading effort without changing the numbers.

blocks.text: A bar chart of city delivery times built during your own exploration can carry gridlines, a border, and precise decimal labels that help you double-check the numbers. The operations manager probably doesn't need any of that to get the point. Gridlines can be deleted from a chart; if precise values matter to the audience, label the data point directly instead of relying on gridlines. Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph.

A chart's border can be removed, since it is not adding informative value; white space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border. Data labels should be used sparingly, only where the exact values are important to the audience; otherwise remove them and use the axis instead. Unnecessary trailing zeroes can be dropped from axis labels — '22.00 minutes' can become '22 min'. Diagonally rotated axis text is slower to read; city-name tick labels like Lagos, Abuja, and Kano don't need to be rotated at all.

None of these changes alter the underlying delivery-time numbers.

steps.title: Decluttering a chart for a non-technical audience
steps.lede: Watch how each removal reduces reading effort. The same design principles apply in any charting tool.

blocks.group_title: Decluttering a chart for a non-technical audience

segments.label: Removing chart clutter: border, gridlines, trailing zeros, diagonal labels, and excess data labels
segments.summary: The presenter opens by explaining that every chart element adds cognitive burden, and that overwhelming an audience risks losing them entirely — establishing why decluttering matters. Working on a bar chart in Excel, they remove the chart border (noting white space does the job of separation better), delete the gridlines and shaded background, then reformat the y-axis to drop trailing zeros by switching to thousands units with a 'k' suffix. They then abbreviate the diagonal month labels on the x-axis to horizontal text, citing research that diagonal text takes fifty percent longer to read. Finally, they weigh whether exact values are needed: deciding they are not, they delete all data labels and keep the y-axis instead, leaving a much cleaner chart.

bridge.before: Watch how each removal reduces reading effort. Note: the presenter uses Excel; the same design principles apply in any charting tool. The clip does not demonstrate labelling a data point directly when precision matters (f1).
bridge.after: The clip shows f2–f6 applied in sequence. Devspace's text also covers f1: when precise values are essential, label the data point directly rather than restoring gridlines.

steps.title: Which elements reduce clutter?
steps.lede: Identify the chart elements that should be removed to simplify a chart for a non-technical audience.

public.prompt: An analyst has a bar chart with a visible border, gridlines, decimal axis labels (e.g. '34.00'), diagonally rotated city-name tick labels, and a data label on every bar. The operations manager does not need exact values. Which set of changes best simplifies this chart?

options.text: Remove the border, gridlines, and data labels; drop trailing zeros from axis labels; display city-name tick labels horizontally.
Remove only the gridlines, because they are the main source of visual noise; keep the border, decimal labels, and data labels to maintain precision.
Keep all elements — removing any of them risks losing information the audience needs to understand the chart.
Remove the data labels and replace them with a table below the chart so the audience can look up exact values.

opt_a.message: Correct. Removing the border, gridlines, trailing zeros, diagonal labels, and unnecessary data labels reduces the visual effort the audience must spend before they can act on the finding.

opt_b.message: Incorrect. Gridlines are one source of clutter, but the border, decimal trailing zeros, and diagonal tick labels also add visual effort without adding informative value. Data labels should be removed when exact values are not critical.

opt_c.message: Incorrect. None of these removals change the underlying data. The border adds no informative value; white space differentiates the chart better. Trailing zeros and diagonal labels slow reading.

opt_d.message: Incorrect. Adding a separate table increases the total visual effort. Since the manager does not need exact values, removing data labels and keeping the axis is the simpler solution.

correct.message: Exactly right. Each removal — border, gridlines, trailing zeros, diagonal labels, excess data labels — reduces the visual effort the audience must spend before they can act on the finding.

incorrect.message: Focus on what each element adds for the audience. The border adds no informative value; white space does the job better. Trailing zeros and diagonal labels slow reading. Data labels are only needed when exact values are critical.

hints: Which elements encode data, and which are just visual decoration?
If the manager does not need exact values, do data labels help or add clutter?

steps.title: Why remove the border?
steps.lede: Explain why removing a chart border improves readability for a non-technical audience.

public.prompt: Why can a chart's border be removed without losing anything important?

options.text: White space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border, and the border is not adding informative value.
The border should only be removed if the chart has no gridlines, because one of the two is needed to frame the chart.
Borders are only decorative in pie charts; bar charts need a border to separate the bars from the background.
Removing the border makes the chart smaller, which saves space on the slide.

opt_a.message: Correct. A chart's border is not adding informative value; white space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border.

opt_b.message: Incorrect. Neither a border nor gridlines are required to frame a chart. White space alone differentiates the chart from surrounding content.

opt_c.message: Incorrect. The principle applies to all chart types: a border is not adding informative value regardless of chart type, and white space does the job of separation better.

opt_d.message: Incorrect. Removing a border does not change the chart's dimensions. The reason to remove it is that it adds no informative value, not that it saves space.

correct.message: Right. The border encodes no data and adds no informative value. White space around the chart separates it from surrounding content just as effectively.

incorrect.message: A chart's border can be removed because it is not adding informative value; white space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border.

hints: Does the border tell the audience anything about the delivery data?
What does white space do that a border also does?

steps.title: Simplify a chart for the operations manager
steps.lede: Given a bar chart with a border, gridlines, trailing-zero axis labels, rotated city-name tick labels, and data labels on every bar — simplify it for a non-technical operations manager.

public.prompt: The operations manager's bar chart currently has these elements. Classify each one: should it be kept as-is, removed, or changed? (The manager does not need exact delivery-time values.)

items.text: Data labels showing '34.00 min', '22.00 min', '19.00 min' on every bar
City-name tick labels 'Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano' displayed diagonally at 45°
The bars themselves (the encoded delivery-time data)

item_gridlines.message: Gridlines can be deleted from a chart. If precise values matter, label the data point directly instead — but here the manager does not need exact values, so the axis alone is sufficient.

item_data_labels.message: Data labels should be used sparingly, only where exact values are important to the audience. Since the manager does not need exact values, remove the data labels and rely on the axis.

item_axis_labels.message: Unnecessary trailing zeros can be dropped — '10.00' becomes '10' or '10 min'. This reduces visual noise without changing the data.

item_tick_labels.message: Diagonally rotated axis text is slower to read. Labels can be abbreviated so they render horizontally — 'Lagos', 'Abuja', and 'Kano' are short enough to display horizontally without overlap.

item_bars.message: The bars encode the delivery-time data — they are the point of the chart and must be kept.

correct.message: Correct. Remove gridlines and unnecessary data labels; drop trailing zeros from axis labels; display city-name tick labels horizontally. The bars stay — they are the data.

incorrect.message: Focus on what each element adds for the audience. Gridlines and excess data labels add visual effort without adding value. Trailing zeros and diagonal labels slow reading. The bars are the data and must stay.

hints: Which elements encode the delivery-time data, and which are just formatting?
If the manager does not need exact values, do data labels help or add clutter?

steps.title: What you've learned
steps.lede: Two skills that work together: matching the chart to the point, then clearing the noise.

blocks.text: Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph. None of these changes alter the underlying delivery-time numbers — only how much visual effort it takes to read them. Match the chart to the point; then strip everything that doesn't serve that point.

remediation_steps.title: Scatterplots: exploratory by default, communicative by design
remediation_steps.lede: A scatterplot is a powerful tool for your own analysis — but it needs extra design work to communicate findings to an audience.

blocks.text: A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. When you plot distance_km against delivery_minutes for orders across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano, you are exploring a relationship — that is the scatterplot's strength. It can still be designed to convey findings to an audience, but that requires deliberate choices: a clear title stating the finding, colour coding by city, and a trend line if the relationship is the point. Without those additions, a scatterplot of 15 order records is harder for the operations manager to read than a bar chart or line graph.

remediation_steps.title: Matching chart type to the point: a quick contrast
remediation_steps.lede: The same delivery data can be shown as a bar chart, line graph, pie chart, or scatterplot — the right choice depends entirely on the point you are making.

blocks.text: Bar chart: comparing values across categories — which city has the longest average delivery time? Use it when the point is a side-by-side comparison (Lagos 34 min, Abuja 22 min, Kano 19 min). Line graph: showing change over time — is Lagos delivery time rising week over week? Pie chart: part-to-whole — does Lagos account for most of total orders? The pie must sum to 100%. Boxplot: comparing distributions side by side — but may be unfamiliar to a non-technical audience, so a bar chart or line plot often makes the point more directly. Scatterplot: exploring a relationship — distance vs. delivery time — but needs extra design work to communicate findings clearly.

It can look like comparing pie slices is just as easy as comparing bar lengths — but it is not. A bar chart's aligned, common baseline makes length differences easy to judge; two pie slices of similar size are harder to rank correctly by eye. Use a pie chart only when the part-to-whole relationship is the point, not when precise comparison between categories is needed.

remediation_steps.title: What counts as clutter — and why removing it helps
remediation_steps.lede: Each element you remove from a chart reduces the cognitive effort the audience spends reading it.

blocks.text: Gridlines can be deleted; if precise values matter, label the data point directly instead. A chart's border can be removed — white space differentiates parts of a visual better than a border. Data labels should be used sparingly, only where exact values are important; otherwise use the axis. Unnecessary trailing zeroes can be dropped from axis labels. Diagonally rotated axis text is slower to read — abbreviate labels so they render horizontally.

Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph. None of these removals change the underlying delivery-time numbers.

remediation_steps.title: Border vs. white space: why the border can go
remediation_steps.lede: A chart border feels like it organises the visual — but white space does that job better.

blocks.text: A chart's border is not adding informative value — it does not encode any data and does not help the audience read the bars. White space around the chart differentiates it from surrounding content just as effectively, without adding a visual element the eye has to process. Removing the border is one of the quickest single changes that reduces clutter on a chart built for a non-technical audience like the operations manager.
